why-navratri-lasts-nine-nights.description: Why Navratri is nine days: the Devi Mahatmyam story, the three goddesses, the nine forms of Durga, and what each night asks of you at home today.
outline: Hook: Navratri lasts nine nights because the Goddess fights for nine nights in the Devi Mahatmyam; the story is really about how long it takes to turn around a stubborn mind.
## Why is Navratri nine days long? — the battle with Mahishasura in the Devi Mahatmyam, and why the victory comes on the tenth day
## Three goddesses, three nights each — Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati as strength, abundance and wisdom; the nine forms of Durga named briefly
## Why Navratri is nine nights in the dark half of the year — new moon of Ashwin, the turn toward winter, the harvest and the nights getting longer
Close: pick one form of the Goddess per night, light one lamp, and notice which quality you most need this season.
takeaways: Navratri lasts nine nights because the Devi Mahatmyam describes the Goddess battling Mahishasura for nine nights and winning on the tenth, Vijayadashami.
The nine nights are often grouped in threes: Durga for strength, Lakshmi for abundance, Saraswati for wisdom, a slow movement from courage to clarity.
Sharad Navratri begins with the new moon of Ashwin, usually in September or October, as the nights grow longer.

faq.q: Why is Navratri celebrated for nine days and not seven or ten?
faq.a: The Devi Mahatmyam, part of the Markandeya Purana, tells of the Goddess fighting the buffalo demon Mahishasura over nine nights. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, marks her victory. Many families also read the nine nights as three sets of three, honouring Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati in turn, which gives the festival a natural rhythm of strength, prosperity and wisdom.

faq.q: What are the nine forms of Durga worshipped in Navratri?
faq.a: In the north Indian tradition the nine forms, or Navadurga, are Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri and Siddhidatri, one for each night. South Indian homes often follow the Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati grouping instead. Both are traditional; you can follow whichever your family knows, or simply honour the Goddess as one each evening.

faq.q: When does Sharad Navratri start each year?
faq.a: Sharad Navratri begins on the first day after the new moon of the lunar month of Ashwin, which usually falls in late September or October. Because the Hindu calendar is lunar, the exact start moves every year. Check the current year's panchangam for your city, since the tithi can shift by a day between India and the United States.

faq.q: What does the Mahishasura story actually mean?
faq.a: Mahishasura was a buffalo demon who could change shape and could not be defeated by any god. The story says only the combined power of all the gods, gathered into one Goddess, could stop him. Read symbolically, he is the dull, stubborn, shape-shifting part of us, and the Goddess is focused energy that finally refuses to negotiate with it.

ayudha-pooja-meaning.description: Ayudha Pooja meaning, simply: why South Indian homes bless tools, books, cars and laptops on Navami, and how to do a small version at your own desk.
secondaryKeywords: why we worship tools on ayudha pooja
outline: Hook: a mechanic's shop on Navami, spanners in a neat row smeared with sandal paste; Ayudha Pooja is the day we thank the things that feed us.
## Ayudha Pooja meaning — worship of instruments, the Mahabharata story of the Pandavas retrieving their weapons from the shami tree, and Saraswati Pooja for books
## Why bless a laptop or a car? — tools as extensions of our effort; the idea that work itself is worship; resting the tools for a day
## A small Ayudha Pooja at home or at your desk — clean, arrange, a dot of kumkum and sandal, a flower, a lamp, and not using them until the next morning
Close: clean one tool you use daily, put a flower on it, and let it rest for one evening.
takeaways: Ayudha Pooja is the day South Indian families honour the tools of their livelihood, from ploughs and spanners to laptops and cars, on Navami of Navratri.
The idea is gratitude: the things that help us work are cleaned, decorated and rested, and work begins afresh on Vijayadashami.

faq.q: Why do we worship tools on Ayudha Pooja?
faq.a: Ayudha means instrument or weapon. The day honours whatever helps you earn, learn and live, from a farmer's plough to a programmer's laptop. Tradition links it to the Pandavas retrieving their weapons from a shami tree after their exile in the Mahabharata. The deeper idea is gratitude: effort needs instruments, and instruments deserve care and a day of rest.

faq.q: Is Ayudha Pooja the same as Saraswati Pooja?
faq.a: In Tamil Nadu and much of South India they fall together on the Navami of Navratri. Books, musical instruments and school bags are placed before Saraswati, while vehicles and tools receive their own blessing. Elsewhere, Saraswati Puja may be observed on a different day of Navratri according to the nakshatra. Many homes simply honour learning and livelihood side by side.

faq.q: Can I do Ayudha Pooja for my laptop and phone at home?
faq.a: Yes, and many working families now do. Wipe the laptop, phone or car clean, place it on a clean cloth, apply a small dot of sandal paste and kumkum where it will not damage anything, offer a flower and light a lamp. Customarily you leave the items unused until the next morning, when work restarts on Vijayadashami.

navratri-fasting-rules.description: Navratri fasting rules explained plainly: what people eat and avoid, why, how to fast safely with work and health, and gentler options that still count.
secondaryKeywords: what to eat during navratri fast
can i drink coffee during navratri fast
outline: Hook: a fast is not a punishment for the body; for nine nights it is a way of making the body lighter so attention can move somewhere else.
## Navratri fasting rules, the common version — no grains, onion, garlic or meat; fruit, milk, sabudana, kuttu, rock salt; one meal or phalahar
## Why these rules? — lightness, season change, sattvic food, and the fast as a daily reminder rather than a feat
## What if you cannot fast fully? — health, pregnancy, medication, demanding jobs; partial fasts, one meal, giving up one thing, and consulting a doctor
Close: choose a fast you can keep kindly for all nine days, and notice how your attention changes by day four.
takeaways: Common Navratri fasting rules avoid grains, onion, garlic, meat and alcohol, and use fruit, milk, sabudana, buckwheat flour and rock salt instead.
A partial fast kept with steady attention is as traditional as a strict one; anyone with a health condition should adapt it with a doctor's advice.

faq.q: What can you eat during a Navratri fast?
faq.a: Most families allow fruits, milk, curd, paneer, nuts, potatoes, sweet potato, sabudana, and flours such as kuttu (buckwheat), singhara (water chestnut) and rajgira (amaranth). Food is cooked with rock salt, ghee or groundnut oil. Grains like rice and wheat, onion, garlic, meat, eggs and alcohol are avoided. Customs differ between regions, so family practice is the best guide.

faq.q: Can I drink coffee or tea during Navratri fast?
faq.a: Many people do drink tea or coffee with milk during a Navratri fast, especially on a fruit-and-milk fast, while stricter observers avoid them as stimulants. There is no single scriptural rule. If you are fasting through a working day, a cup of tea may be what keeps the fast gentle. Decide once at the start and stay consistent.

faq.q: Is it okay to fast for only some days of Navratri?
faq.a: Yes. Many devotees fast on the first and last days, or on Ashtami alone, and eat simply on the others. Others give up one thing, such as grains or sweets, for all nine nights. The tradition values sincerity and steadiness over severity. People with diabetes, pregnancy or other health needs should shape any fast with their doctor.

dussehra-ravana-story-meaning.description: Dussehra significance, told through Ravana and Durga: why the tenth day marks victory, what burning the effigy means, and why Ravana is more than a villain.
outline: Hook: on Dussehra we burn a ten-headed man who was, the story says, a great scholar and devotee of Shiva; so what exactly are we burning?
## Why is Dussehra celebrated? — two stories on one day: Rama's victory over Ravana in the Ramayana and Durga's victory over Mahishasura in the Devi Mahatmyam
## Dussehra significance: what the ten heads stand for — Ravana as learning without humility; the heads read as ten attachments or passions
## Vijayadashami as a beginning — shami leaves, Vidyarambham, starting new learning; the victory is quiet and daily
Close: name one 'head' you would like to put down, and begin one small new thing on Vijayadashami.
takeaways: Dussehra, or Vijayadashami, marks two victories: Rama over Ravana in the Ramayana, and Durga over Mahishasura in the Devi Mahatmyam, on the tenth day after Navratri begins.
Ravana is burned not because he was ignorant but because he was brilliant and arrogant; the effigy stands for knowledge that forgot humility.

faq.q: Why is Dussehra celebrated?
faq.a: Dussehra celebrates victory. In north India it marks Rama defeating Ravana, as told in the Ramayana, and effigies of Ravana are burned. In Bengal and much of the east it closes Durga Puja, marking the Goddess's victory over Mahishasura from the Devi Mahatmyam. In the south it is Vijayadashami, an auspicious day to begin learning, music or new work.

faq.q: What do Ravana's ten heads symbolise?
faq.a: Traditionally the ten heads show Ravana's vast learning; he was said to know the four Vedas and six shastras. Later teachers read them as ten weaknesses such as lust, anger, greed, pride, jealousy and attachment. Either way the point is similar: great capacity without humility becomes dangerous. Burning the effigy is a public reminder to burn those tendencies privately.

faq.q: Is Vijayadashami the same day as Dussehra?
faq.a: Yes, they are two names for the same festival, the tenth day of the bright half of Ashwin, right after the nine nights of Navratri. Some regions observe it a day apart depending on when the Dashami tithi falls. Check the current year's panchangam for your city if you want the precise day and the auspicious Vijay muhurat.

why-is-diwali-celebrated.description: Why is Diwali celebrated? Rama's return, Krishna and Narakasura, Lakshmi's arrival and Mahavira's liberation: four stories and the one light they share.
secondaryKeywords: why do we light diyas on diwali
outline: Hook: ask four Indian families why Diwali is celebrated and you may get four different stories, and every one of them ends with a lamp.
## Why is Diwali celebrated in the north? — Rama's return to Ayodhya after fourteen years, the city lit with rows of lamps, as told in Ramayana traditions
## Deepavali in the south and the other stories — Krishna and Satyabhama defeating Narakasura in the Bhagavata Purana; Lakshmi emerging from the churning ocean; Jain and Sikh observances
## What do all the stories share? — return, rescue, abundance and release; darkness of the new moon of Karthika met with small flames
Close: tell your household one Diwali story this season, and light the first lamp together while telling it.
takeaways: Diwali is celebrated for several reasons: Rama's homecoming to Ayodhya, Krishna's victory over Narakasura, Lakshmi's arrival from the cosmic ocean, and Mahavira's liberation in the Jain tradition.
It falls on the new-moon night of Karthika (Ashwin in some calendars), usually late October or November, so its lamps light the darkest night of the month.

faq.q: What is the main story behind Diwali?
faq.a: In north India the best-known story is Rama returning to Ayodhya after fourteen years of exile and defeating Ravana; the city lit rows of lamps to welcome him. In Tamil Nadu and much of the south, Deepavali honours Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura. Lakshmi Puja on the same night celebrates the goddess of abundance. All are traditional.

faq.q: Why is Diwali called the festival of lights?
faq.a: The name Deepavali means a row of lamps. It falls on the new moon, the darkest night of the lunar month, and homes are lit with clay oil lamps, candles and electric lights. The lamp is a symbol of knowledge pushing back ignorance, and of welcoming Lakshmi and returning heroes home. The light is the one element every Diwali story shares.

faq.q: How can I explain the Diwali story to kids simply?
faq.a: Try this: a good prince named Rama was sent away from home for many years. He rescued his wife Sita from a demon king and finally came home. The whole city was so happy they lit lamps on every doorstep so he could find his way in the dark. That is why we light lamps: to welcome goodness home.

five-days-of-diwali.description: The five days of Diwali explained day by day, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj: what each day honours and one simple thing to do at home on each of the five days.
outline: Hook: Diwali is not one night but a five-day arc, and if you treat it like five small practices instead of one big party, it lands differently in the body.
## The five days of Diwali at a glance — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi Puja on Amavasya, Govardhan Puja, Bhai Dooj
## What does each day ask of you? — Dhanteras and Dhanvantari (health before wealth), the pre-dawn oil bath, the evening lamp, gratitude to the land, the sibling bond
## A simple practice for each day — clean one space, oil bath and early rise, lamps at dusk, feed someone, call a sibling
Close: write the five days on a note on your fridge and do one small act each day; that is the whole festival.
takeaways: The five days of Diwali are Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi Puja on the new moon, Govardhan Puja and Bhai Dooj, each with its own focus.
Dhanteras honours Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, a reminder that tradition places health before wealth at the start of the festival.

faq.q: What are the five days of Diwali called?
faq.a: The five days are Dhanteras (Dhanvantari Trayodashi), Naraka Chaturdashi (Choti Diwali), Lakshmi Puja on Amavasya, the new moon, then Govardhan Puja or Annakut, and finally Bhai Dooj. Regions emphasise different days. In Tamil Nadu, Deepavali itself is observed on Naraka Chaturdashi with a pre-dawn oil bath, and Lakshmi Puja may fall on the same day.

faq.q: What is the meaning of Dhanteras?
faq.a: Dhanteras comes from dhana, wealth, and teras, the thirteenth lunar day. It honours Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, who emerged from the churning of the ocean holding a pot of amrita. People buy metal utensils or gold, but the older emphasis is health: the festival of prosperity begins by honouring the source of healing.

faq.q: What do you do on Govardhan Puja and Bhai Dooj?
faq.a: On Govardhan Puja families remember Krishna lifting Govardhan hill to shelter villagers from storms, from the Bhagavata Purana, and offer a mountain of food called Annakut. On Bhai Dooj sisters apply a tilak to their brothers and pray for their long life, recalling Yamuna feeding her brother Yama. Both days are about gratitude and protection.

naraka-chaturdashi-oil-bath.description: Naraka Chaturdashi and the Deepavali oil bath: the Narakasura story, why Tamil families rise before dawn for Ganga snanam, and keeping it far from home.
outline: Hook: the smell of warm sesame oil in the dark, a grandmother's thumb pressing oil into your scalp, crackers somewhere down the street: that is Deepavali morning in a Tamil house.
## What is Naraka Chaturdashi? — Krishna and Satyabhama defeating Narakasura in the Bhagavata Purana; Narakasura's wish that the day be remembered with light
## Why the pre-dawn oil bath? — 'Ganga snanam aachaa?' as the greeting; the belief that Ganga is present in all water that morning; oil, shikakai, new clothes
## Keeping the oil bath when you live far away — a quiet version before work, a video call to parents, lehiyam and sweets
Close: wake a little earlier that morning, oil your hair, bathe slowly, and greet one person with 'Ganga snanam aachaa?'
takeaways: Naraka Chaturdashi remembers Krishna and Satyabhama defeating the demon Narakasura; in Tamil Nadu it is Deepavali day itself, begun with a pre-dawn oil bath.
The oil bath is called Ganga snanam because tradition holds that the Ganga is present in all water at dawn on this day.

faq.q: Why do we take an oil bath on Deepavali?
faq.a: In South Indian tradition the pre-dawn oil bath on Naraka Chaturdashi is called Ganga snanam, because the Ganga is believed to be present in all water that morning. Warm sesame oil is massaged into the head and body, washed off with shikakai or herbal powder, and followed by new clothes. It marks cleansing after Narakasura's defeat and the start of the festival.

faq.q: What is the story of Narakasura?
faq.a: The Bhagavata Purana tells of Narakasura, a powerful demon who imprisoned thousands of women and terrorised the heavens. Krishna, with his wife Satyabhama driving his chariot, defeated him. Some tellings say Satyabhama herself struck the final blow. Before dying, Narakasura asked that his death be remembered with lamps and celebration, which is why the day opens Deepavali.

faq.q: Is Naraka Chaturdashi the same day as Diwali?
faq.a: In Tamil Nadu and much of South India, Deepavali is celebrated on Naraka Chaturdashi, often a day before the north Indian Lakshmi Puja, though some years they coincide. In the north it is called Choti Diwali, the day before the main night. The exact day depends on the tithi, so check the current year's panchangam for your city.

karthigai-deepam-significance.description: Karthigai Deepam significance: the Shiva Purana story of the endless column of fire, why Tiruvannamalai lights a beacon, and what the flame asks of us.
outline: Hook: Brahma and Vishnu once argued over who was greater, and a pillar of fire appeared that neither could find the end of; Karthigai Deepam is the night we remember that pillar.
## Karthigai Deepam significance: the column of fire — the Shiva Purana story of the Jyotirlinga; Brahma's swan, Vishnu's boar; the lie of the ketaki flower
## Why is the flame lit on a hill? — Arunachala at Tiruvannamalai as that fire become mountain; the Maha Deepam lit at dusk; Murugan and the six Karthigai maidens
## What is the story really about? — ego searching for limits in something limitless; the lamp as a small, humble version of the infinite flame
Close: at dusk on Karthigai Deepam, light one lamp, look at it for a full minute, and let the argument in your head end there.
takeaways: Karthigai Deepam recalls the Shiva Purana story of Shiva appearing as an endless column of fire that neither Brahma nor Vishnu could measure.
It falls on the Karthigai nakshatra in the Tamil month of Karthigai, around November or December, when the Maha Deepam is lit atop Arunachala hill.

faq.q: What is the story behind Karthigai Deepam?
faq.a: The Shiva Purana tells of Brahma and Vishnu arguing over who was supreme. A boundless pillar of fire appeared. Vishnu became a boar and dug down, Brahma became a swan and flew up; neither found its end. Vishnu admitted it, Brahma lied. The fire was Shiva. At Tiruvannamalai, the hill Arunachala is revered as that fire made solid.

faq.q: Why is Karthigai Deepam celebrated in Tamil Nadu?
faq.a: Karthigai Deepam is one of the oldest Tamil festivals of light, mentioned in Sangam-era poetry. It honours Shiva as the column of fire and also Murugan, who was raised by the six Karthigai maidens, the stars of the Pleiades. Homes are lit with rows of clay agal vilakku lamps, and a great beacon is lit on Arunachala hill.

faq.q: When is Karthigai Deepam celebrated?
faq.a: Karthigai Deepam falls on the day the Moon is in the Karthigai nakshatra (Krittika, the Pleiades) during the Tamil month of Karthigai, usually close to the full moon, around November or December. The exact date moves each year with the lunar calendar, so check the current year's panchangam, especially if you live outside India.

secondaryKeywords: how to celebrate karthigai deepam at home
outline: Hook: lighting forty small lamps one after another is a strange, slowing thing to do; by the twentieth your breath has changed.
## Karthigai Deepam at home: what you need — clay agal vilakku, sesame oil or ghee, cotton wicks, a tray; where to place them (threshold, windows, puja corner)
## How many lamps, and in what order? — traditions of lamps in rows, odd numbers, starting at the puja lamp and moving outward to the doorway
## Pori, appam and the evening itself — puffed-rice pori urundai with jaggery, nei appam, lighting at dusk, simple safety in apartments
Close: light the lamps slowly, one breath per lamp, and sit with them until the first one burns low.
takeaways: To celebrate Karthigai Deepam at home, light rows of clay agal vilakku lamps at dusk, from the puja lamp outward to the front door and windows.
Lighting many lamps one by one works as a practice of attention; offerings of pori urundai and nei appam complete the evening.

faq.q: How do you celebrate Karthigai Deepam at home?
faq.a: Clean the home, draw a kolam at the entrance, and at dusk light clay agal vilakku lamps filled with sesame oil or ghee, starting from the lamp in your puja corner and moving to the threshold, steps and windows. Offer pori urundai, nei appam or adai, say a simple prayer to Shiva or Murugan, and let the lamps burn into the night.

faq.q: How many lamps should be lit on Karthigai Deepam?
faq.a: There is no fixed number. Many families light lamps in rows at every doorway and window, often choosing odd numbers such as nine, twenty-seven or more. Some light the lamps for three evenings, from the day before to the day after. Light as many as you can watch safely; attention matters more than the count.

faq.q: What is Karthigai pori and why is it offered?
faq.a: Pori is puffed rice, mixed with melted jaggery, cardamom and sometimes coconut, then shaped into balls called pori urundai. It is the traditional offering on Karthigai Deepam, alongside nei appam and vella adai. Puffed rice is light and bursts open in heat, which many read as a symbol of the self opening in the presence of the flame.

tiruvannamalai-deepam-from-afar.description: Tiruvannamalai Deepam, watched from far away: an NRI reflection on the Arunachala beacon, livestreams at odd US hours, and lighting one lamp to join in.
outline: Hook: a phone propped against the sugar jar at 7:30 in the morning in New Jersey, a livestream from Tiruvannamalai, and a mother on the other line saying 'there, there, it's lit'.
## What is the Tiruvannamalai Deepam? — the Maha Deepam lit on Arunachala at dusk; the Bharani Deepam at dawn in the temple; the hill as Shiva
## Watching from another time zone — IST dusk as a US morning; livestreams, parents on video, the odd intimacy of a festival on a small screen
## Can you take part without being there? — lighting a lamp at the same moment, the Tamil phrase 'Annamalaiyarukku arohara', giri valam as an inner walk
Close: find out when the beacon is lit in IST, set an alarm, and light one lamp in your kitchen at that moment.
takeaways: The Tiruvannamalai Deepam is a great beacon lit atop Arunachala hill at dusk on Karthigai Deepam, honouring Shiva as the endless column of fire.
From the US, that dusk in India usually falls in your early morning; lighting a lamp as the livestream shows the flame is a simple way to join.

faq.q: What time is the Tiruvannamalai Deepam lit, and can I watch it live from the US?
faq.a: The Maha Deepam is lit on the summit of Arunachala around sunset in India, roughly six in the evening IST, on Karthigai Deepam day. On the US East Coast that is usually early morning, and on the West Coast late the previous night. Many channels livestream it; check the current year's panchangam and the temple's announcements for exact timing.

faq.q: What is the difference between Bharani Deepam and Maha Deepam?
faq.a: Bharani Deepam is lit before dawn inside the Arunachaleswarar temple, when five lamps are lit from one flame and later merged back, symbolising the many arising from the one. Maha Deepam is lit at dusk on the hilltop in a huge cauldron of ghee and can be seen for miles. Together they frame the festival day.

faq.q: How can I celebrate Karthigai Deepam in the USA?
faq.a: Light clay lamps or tea lights at your door and windows at dusk on the day, draw a small kolam, and offer pori or any simple sweet. If you can, light one lamp at the moment the Maha Deepam is lit in Tiruvannamalai while watching the livestream. Local Hindu temples in larger US cities often hold their own Deepam.

outline: Hook: six days, one meal, one chant, one small shift in how you use your hunger; that is the whole Skanda Sashti fast, and it is enough.
## How does the Skanda Sashti fast work? — six days from the Pratipada after Deepavali to Sashti, Soorasamharam on the last day, breaking the fast after
## Skanda Sashti fasting options — full fast, one meal a day, fruit and milk, giving up one food; sattvic food; staying hydrated

You can keep it as a full fast, one meal a day, or fruit and milk; consistency across six days matters more than severity.

faq.q: What are the rules of Kanda Sashti viratham?
faq.a: The Kanda Sashti viratham runs for six days in the Tamil month of Aippasi, from the day after the new moon to Sashti. Devotees eat once a day or only fruit and milk, avoid onion, garlic and meat, recite the Kanda Sashti Kavacham, and visit a Murugan temple if they can. The fast ends after Soorasamharam, usually the next morning.

faq.q: What can I eat during the Skanda Sashti fast?
faq.a: Common choices are fruits, milk, buttermilk, tender coconut water and one simple vegetarian meal a day without onion or garlic. Some devotees take only water until evening. There is no single rule. Anyone who is pregnant, diabetic, on medication or doing physical work should keep a lighter version and speak to a doctor before fasting.

faq.q: Why is Skanda Sashti celebrated for six days?
faq.a: Six is Murugan's number. He has six faces as Shanmukha, was nurtured by the six Karthigai maidens, and has six sacred abodes, the Arupadai Veedu. The Skanda Purana describes his battle with the asura Surapadman, which ends on the sixth day, Sashti. The six-day fast mirrors that battle, ending with Soorasamharam.

In the Skanda Purana, the defeated demon becomes Murugan's peacock and rooster: the story transforms the ego rather than destroying it.

faq.q: What is the story of Soorasamharam?
faq.a: The Skanda Purana tells of Surapadman, an asura who won a boon of near invincibility and oppressed the gods. Murugan, born from sparks of Shiva's third eye, received the vel, a spear, from Parvati and fought him for six days. On the last day Surapadman became a mango tree; Murugan split it with the vel, and the halves became a peacock and a rooster.

faq.q: Why is the peacock Murugan's vehicle?
faq.a: According to the Soorasamharam story, one half of the defeated Surapadman became the peacock that Murugan rides, and the other became the rooster on his banner. Symbolically, the proud, restless ego is not destroyed but tamed and put to work. The peacock, beautiful and vain, now carries wisdom instead of fighting it.

faq.q: Where is Soorasamharam celebrated?
faq.a: Soorasamharam is celebrated in Murugan temples across Tamil Nadu and wherever Tamil communities live, including Malaysia, Singapore, Sri Lanka and the United States. The most famous re-enactment is on the beach at Tiruchendur, one of the six abodes of Murugan, where the battle is traditionally said to have taken place. It falls on Sashti tithi in Aippasi.

faq.q: What is Thaipusam and why is it celebrated?
faq.a: Thaipusam is a festival for Murugan on the day the Moon is in the Poosam nakshatra during the Tamil month of Thai, usually January or February. Tradition says Parvati gave Murugan his vel on this day to defeat the asura Surapadman. It is celebrated at Palani and other Murugan temples, and on a large scale by Tamil communities in Malaysia and Singapore.

faq.q: What is the Idumban kavadi story?
faq.a: Idumban was asked by sage Agastya to carry two hills, Sivagiri and Sakthigiri, to the south. He hung them from a pole across his shoulders. At Palani the load became immovable because the young Murugan stood on one hill. After a playful struggle, Murugan blessed Idumban and declared that anyone carrying a kavadi to him would be blessed.

faq.q: Why do devotees carry kavadi on Thaipusam?
faq.a: Carrying a kavadi, a decorated arch or pots of milk borne on the shoulders, fulfils a vow made to Murugan, often after a prayer was answered or during a hardship. Devotees usually fast and keep discipline beforehand. The meaning is that the burden is offered to the deity: it is still carried, but it is carried as devotion.

faq.q: Why is Pongal celebrated in Tamil Nadu?
faq.a: Pongal is a harvest festival that thanks Surya, the sun, and the forces that make farming possible. It falls as the sun enters Makara, the start of the Tamil month of Thai, around mid-January, after the rice harvest. The name comes from the dish of new rice and milk that is boiled until it overflows, a sign of abundance.

faq.q: What are the four days of Pongal?
faq.a: Bhogi comes first, when old things are discarded and Indra, the rain god, is honoured. Thai Pongal is the main day, for Surya. Mattu Pongal honours cattle, which are bathed, decorated and fed. Kaanum Pongal is for visiting family and outings. Each day thanks a different part of the web that makes a harvest possible.

faq.q: What is the story behind Mattu Pongal?
faq.a: A popular story says Shiva sent his bull Nandi to earth with a message that people should bathe daily and eat once a month. Nandi mixed it up and said eat daily and bathe once a month. As punishment Shiva sent him to help humans plough fields for the food they now needed. Mattu Pongal thanks cattle for that work.

faq.q: How can I celebrate Pongal at home in the USA?
faq.a: Clean the kitchen, draw a kolam with chalk or rice flour at the door, and cook new rice in milk in a pot tied with turmeric leaves if you can find them. When it boils over, everyone says 'Pongalo Pongal'. Offer sakkarai pongal to the sun, facing east if possible, then share it. Local Tamil associations often hold community Pongal events too.

faq.q: Can I do Pongal pooja without a priest?
faq.a: Yes. Pongal has always been a household festival led by the family. Set up a simple offering to Surya with the pongal, sugarcane or a banana, turmeric, a lamp and some flowers. faq.q: What is the difference between ven pongal and sakkarai pongal?

Sesame and jaggery are eaten because they are warming winter foods, and sharing them is a gesture of speaking sweetly to one another.

faq.q: What is the meaning of Makar Sankranti?
faq.a: Sankranti means the sun's movement from one zodiac sign to the next. Makar Sankranti is when it enters Makara, Capricorn, around mid-January, beginning Uttarayana, the sun's six-month northward course. It is one of the few Hindu festivals fixed by the solar calendar, so its date barely moves. It is celebrated as Pongal, Lohri, Uttarayan and Bihu across India.

faq.q: Why do we eat til and jaggery on Sankranti?
faq.a: Sesame and jaggery are warming, energy-dense foods suited to the cold of mid-winter, and both appear in Ayurvedic winter diets. In Maharashtra people exchange til-gul saying 'til gul ghya, god god bola', take this sweet and speak sweetly. So the food carries two ideas: care for the body in winter and sweetness in relationships.

faq.q: What is the significance of Uttarayan?
faq.a: Uttarayana is the half of the year when the sun appears to move northward, from Makar Sankranti to around the summer solstice. Tradition treats it as auspicious; in the Mahabharata, Bhishma waits on his bed of arrows until Uttarayana begins before leaving his body. In Gujarat, Uttarayan is celebrated with kite flying across rooftops.

faq.q: What is the meaning of Maha Shivaratri?
faq.a: Maha Shivaratri means the great night of Shiva. It falls on the Chaturdashi, the fourteenth night, of the dark fortnight in the month of Magha by the South Indian calendar, or Phalguna in the north, usually in February or March. Devotees fast, offer bilva leaves and water to the Shiva linga, chant, and keep a vigil through the night.

faq.q: Why do we stay awake on Shivaratri?
faq.a: The Shiva Purana tells of a hunter who stayed awake all night in a bilva tree, unknowingly dropping leaves on a Shiva linga below, and was blessed. The vigil, jagarana, is divided into four prahara pujas. Symbolically, staying awake on the darkest night is about alertness: remaining conscious when everything invites sleep and forgetting.

faq.q: What stories are associated with Maha Shivaratri?
faq.a: Several. It is said to be the night Shiva appeared as the infinite column of fire, the night of his marriage to Parvati, and the night he performed the Tandava, the cosmic dance. Some link it to Shiva swallowing the poison from the churning of the ocean. Different regions emphasise different stories; the night honours them all.

faq.q: How do you do Shivaratri puja at home?
faq.a: Clean your puja space before sunset and set up a small Shiva linga or picture. Offer water, then milk, curd, honey or just water again, followed by bilva or other leaves, flowers and a lamp. faq.q: What is the four prahara puja on Shivaratri?
faq.a: The night of Shivaratri is divided into four praharas, watches of roughly three hours each, from sunset to sunrise. In temples a separate abhishekam is performed in each, often with milk, curd, ghee and honey in turn. At home you can do a brief offering and chant at the start of each prahara and meditate or read in between.

faq.q: What can I eat during the Shivaratri fast?
faq.a: Strict observers take only water through the day and night. Many others eat fruit, milk, nuts, sabudana or a single simple meal without grains, onion or garlic, breaking the fast after the morning puja the next day. Anyone with a health condition, pregnancy or medication should keep a gentle fast and ask a doctor before going without food.

faq.q: How can I observe Shivaratri while working?
faq.a: Keep what is essential and let the rest bend. Eat lightly or keep a fruit fast through the workday if your health allows. In the evening, offer water and a leaf or flower to a Shiva linga or picture, light a lamp and chant Om Namah Shivaya. Stay awake as long as you honestly can, perhaps through one prahara.

faq.q: Is it okay to sleep on Shivaratri night?
faq.a: Tradition encourages staying awake, but no one is judged for their body's limits. Many devotees keep vigil until midnight, the most important time, and then rest. Others wake before dawn for the last prahara. If you must sleep, sleep after a sincere offering and a quiet sitting. The alertness you bring matters more than the hours.

faq.q: What is the simplest way to celebrate Shivaratri at home?

The next morning's colours recall Krishna's play with Radha in Braj; Holi falls on the full moon of Phalguna, usually in March.

faq.q: What is the story behind Holika Dahan?
faq.a: In the Bhagavata Purana, the demon king Hiranyakashipu demanded everyone worship him, but his son Prahlad stayed devoted to Vishnu. The king's sister Holika, who could not be harmed by fire, sat in a pyre with Prahlad on her lap. She burned; Prahlad walked out unharmed. The Holika Dahan bonfire on the eve of Holi remembers this.

faq.q: Why is Holi celebrated with colours?
faq.a: The colours come from Krishna's story in Braj. Tradition says the dark-skinned Krishna worried that fair Radha would not like him, and his mother Yashoda playfully suggested he colour her face. Holi in Mathura and Vrindavan still re-enacts that play. More broadly, colour marks spring and the one day when age, caste and status are set aside in fun.

faq.q: How is Narasimha connected to Holi?
faq.a: After the Holika episode, Hiranyakashipu's boon said he could be killed neither by man nor beast, neither by day nor night, neither indoors nor outdoors. Vishnu appeared as Narasimha, half man, half lion, at dusk, on the threshold of the palace, and ended his tyranny. Holi's story therefore honours Prahlad's faith and Vishnu's protection together.

faq.q: How can I do Holika Dahan puja at home?
faq.a: On the evening of Holika Dahan, clean a safe spot and light a large ghee lamp or a small contained fire in a metal or clay vessel. Offer turmeric, kumkum, roasted grains, a coconut or jaggery. faq.q: What do you offer in the Holika Dahan fire?
faq.a: Traditional offerings include roasted wheat or barley ears, grams, coconut, jaggery, turmeric, kumkum, raw cotton thread wound around the pyre, and cow-dung cakes. Some families roast new grain in the fire and eat it as prasad. A personal practice is to write down a habit or grudge and offer that too, symbolically burning it.

faq.q: Is it safe to light a Holika fire in an apartment?
faq.a: An open bonfire indoors is not safe and may break building rules. Instead, use a large oil or ghee lamp, or a small flame in a sturdy metal or clay vessel on a balcony, away from curtains and with water at hand. The meaning lies in the intention and the circling, not in the size of the fire.

outline: Hook: a university quad in March, half the crowd has never heard of Prahlad, and yet everyone is laughing with pink faces; I stood there wondering whether that was Holi or something else.

## Is it still Holi if nobody knows the story? — a line from Surdas on Krishna's play; colour as invitation, story as roots

Close: this Holi, bring one person who has never played, and tell them the story in two sentences before the colour flies.
takeaways: Holi in the USA is often celebrated on the nearest weekend at temples and campuses, since the full moon of Phalguna rarely falls on a day off.
Telling the Prahlad and Holika story, even in two sentences, turns a colour party into a festival with roots.

faq.q: How is Holi celebrated in the USA?
faq.a: Many US temples, Indian associations and universities host Holi on the nearest weekend to the Phalguna full moon, with colour play on lawns, music, food and sometimes a small Holika bonfire where permitted. Families also mark the evening before at home with a lamp and prayer. Weather in March can be cold, so some events move to April.

faq.q: How do I explain Holi to American friends?
faq.a: Keep it simple: Holi is a Hindu spring festival. The night before, a bonfire recalls a boy named Prahlad whose faith protected him from fire. The next day people throw coloured powder, remembering Krishna's playfulness, and for a day age and status do not matter. Invite them to wear old white clothes and say 'Happy Holi'.

faq.q: Is the colour powder used for Holi safe for skin?
faq.a: Traditional gulal was made from flowers and herbs like marigold, turmeric and beetroot. Some cheaper powders today contain synthetic dyes that can irritate skin and eyes. Look for powders labelled natural or skin-safe, oil your skin and hair beforehand, protect eyes, and keep it away from young children's faces. Or make your own from turmeric and flowers.
